query: Consider noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and targeted in a single-phase solid-solution state. Their crystal structure is difficult to control at fixed composition, while unsuccessful formation can involve phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures under synthesis regimes with rapid heating and cooling. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs formation and crystal-structure selection in this regime and why? Define a controlled intervention without specifying a technique, predict the observations relative to the initial single-phase baseline, identify the applicable compositional and processing boundaries, cite supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The formation and crystal-structure selection of noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles are governed by the interplay between thermal stress, surface diffusion, and the mixing enthalpies of the constituent elements.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase solid-solution state with more than five elements
generation.conditions: Rapid heating and cooling synthesis regimes
generation.mechanism: Thermal stress-assisted formation of nanoparticles, influenced by the mixing enthalpies of the constituent elements
generation.predicted_outcome: The formation of single-phase nanoparticles with a face-centered-cubic (FCC) or hexagonal close-packed (HCP) crystal structure, depending on the composition and processing conditions
generation.baseline: Unsuccessful formation involving phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures
generation.boundary: Compositional boundaries: more than five elements, including noble metals; Processing boundaries: rapid heating and cooling synthesis regimes
generation.uncertainty: The exact role of surface diffusion in the formation of nanoparticles, and the influence of other factors such as lattice distortion and cocktail effects

falsification_experiment.design: In situ X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) and X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) experiments to monitor the formation of nanoparticles under different heating and cooling conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the formation of single-phase nanoparticles is not observed under the predicted conditions, or if the crystal structure of the nanoparticles does not match the predicted outcome, the hypothesis is falsified

## Abstract
In this work, for the first time, the thermal stress-assisted formation of submicron pillars (SPs) from a high entropy alloy (HEA) thin film is made possible, and novel molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are proposed to assess the underlying mechanisms. In a series of experiments, the growth of quasi-equiatomic HEA SPs from CoCrCuFeNi HEA thin films was demonstrated under different heating and cooling conditions. Atomistic simulations are performed to probe possible formation mechanisms in two ways. One is to first obtain surface elastic constants and then conduct surface stability analysis with the consideration of size-dependent surface stress. The other is to effectively apply large compressive stress while simplifying the molecular dynamics (MD) model by using the Stoney equation to perform long-term MD simulations. From the former, it is suggested that surface diffusion is likely not the dominant cause for the observed pillar formation. From the latter, it is revealed that the level of compressive stress plays a much greater role than the crystalline structure of the film sample. Compared with bulk counterparts, nanostructured HEA materials could be even more fascinating in terms of further enhanced mechanical performance, enhanced damage tolerance and other superior properties that bulk counterparts do not possess. To our knowledge, at least three types of nanostructures, namely, HEA nanopillars, nanoporous HEA and HEA nanoparticles have been successfully fabricated. NbMoTaW HEA nanopillars were successfully fabricated by using focused ion beams (FIB) to mill small-scale pillars (SPs). Due to the well-known size effect in nanomaterials, as predicted, such HEA pillar showed much higher yield strength than that of its bulk form. A method for making HEA nanoparticles with up to eight different elements has been developed, which relied on shocking metal salt-covered carbon nanofibers and followed by rapid quenching. Combined experimental and theoretical studies that utilize the predictions from computational screenings are still scarce and mainly focus on thin film catalyst materials prepared by magnetron sputtering that can be more easily performed in experimental high throughput screening studies. To be able to predict and simulate the variety of binding sites of the different elements present in a HEA, single-phase materials are crucial. If phase segregation occurs, the surface atoms are not randomly distributed anymore and the key assumption of the computational modeling is not valid. Thus the experimental and computational trends will diverge.
HEAs are conventionally prepared as bulk materials employing high-temperature methods such as arc melting. Bulk materials have very low dispersion, i.e., a low ratio of surface to bulk atoms. A large surface-to-bulk atom ratio is, however, vital for efficient catalysts. Nanoparticles possess such high dispersion. This generates a large interest in developing HEA nanoparticle synthesis methods. Comparing multimetallic precursor mixtures with bimetallic ones, we propose a model for the formation of single-phase nanoparticles. The essential conclusion of the model, i.e., that combining multiple elements favors the formation of single-phase nanoparticles, will aid the design of future studies combining experimental investigations with computational simulations.
## Material synthesis
All samples were prepared following a literature procedure described by Yusenko et al. All compounds were prepared from commercial metal precursors (Sigma Aldrich). As cationic precursors the chloropentaammine metal chlorides of Ir, Rh, and Ru were used; Ir(NH3)5Cl]Cl2, [Rh(NH3)5Cl]Cl2, and [Ru(NH3)5Cl]Cl2. The anionic precursors were the ammonium hexachlorometallates of Ir, Pt, and Os; (NH4)2[IrCl6], (NH4)2[PtCl6], and (NH4)2[OsCl6]. In short, separate aqueous solutions of anionic metal precursors (hexachlorates) and cationic metal precursors (chloropentaamines) were prepared by dissolving the respective amounts of the individual metal salts in hot MilliQ water (90 °C). For ex situ characterization, alloy samples were prepared by thermal decomposition of the prepared crystalline single source-precursors in a reducing gas atmosphere (Carbagas, 5% H2 in Ar). The samples were calcined in a quartz-tube furnace (Gero SR-A 40-250/11) in quartz crucibles at 700 °C for 60 minutes (heating ramp 50 K min−1). The crystalline phases of the prepared samples were determined from powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) data using a STOE StadiP with a Cu Kα X-ray source in transmission geometry. The elemental composition was analyzed by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) using a Zeiss Gemini 450 scanning electron microscope equipped with an Oxford Instruments UltimMax 65 EDX detector.
Synchrotron X-ray powder diffraction and X-ray total scattering data for pair distribution function (PDF) analysis of the prepared high entropy alloy samples was collected at DESY P21.1 at PETRAIII; DESY in Hamburg, Germany, with a wavelength of 0.12224 Å. All ex situ samples were prepared as powders in Kapton capillaries and data was collected at room temperature under a helium atmosphere to limit the background contribution arising from air scattering.

The calculations used the revised Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (RPBE) exchange–correlation functional as implemented in the GPAW code. Each system was calculated as both fcc and hcp structures containing 32 and 16 atoms per cell, respectively.
